summaryEn: Taiwan's second-largest mobile operator, and the only one that also owns a major e-commerce business. That makes its gross margin look far worse than its rivals' and its return on equity better — a distinction worth understanding before comparing any of the three carriers.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; telecom framing — the Taiwan Star merger, widest 5G 3.5GHz holding, Jan–Apr operating profit +17% / net profit +19%, three growth engines and the GMI Cloud partnership credited, but the ~100% payout leaving nothing retained, a 57.77% debt ratio and 3.79× book flagged, and — most importantly — the 21.6% gross margin explained as an artefact of consolidating momo's low-margin e-commerce revenue rather than as telecom weakness, so the comparison with FarEasTone is not made incorrectly; sector Communications & Networking → Telecommunications & E-Commerce)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Taiwan Mobile (台灣大哥大, TWSE: 3045) is Taiwan's second-largest mobile operator and the only one of the three that also owns a major **e-commerce business**. Founded in **1997** and **listed in August 2002**, it **merged with Taiwan Star on 1 December 2023**, taking Taiwan's mobile market from five operators to three and giving it **100 MHz in the 5G 3.5GHz band — the widest holding of any carrier**. It also consolidates **momo (8454)**, Taiwan's largest business-to-consumer e-commerce platform, which is profiled separately in this collection.

**That ownership is the single most important thing to understand before reading its accounts.** Taiwan Mobile's gross margin is **21.6%**, against **33.0% at FarEasTone**. This does **not** mean its telecom business is a third less profitable. It means **momo's large, low-margin e-commerce revenue is consolidated into the group** — retail merchandise revenue carries a fraction of the margin that mobile subscriptions do. Comparing the two carriers' gross margins directly is simply a mistake, and one that is easy to make.

Looked at where it matters, the company is performing well. Annual EPS ran **NT$3.91 (FY2022) → 4.33 → 4.57 (FY2024) → NT$4.77 (FY2025)**, with **2026Q1 at NT$1.37, up 13%**. For **January–April 2026, revenue reached NT$65.45bn with operating profit up 17% to NT$7.92bn and net profit up 19% to NT$5.57bn (EPS NT$1.84)**. **Trailing return on equity is 16.61%** — higher than FarEasTone's 14.35%. Operating margin has climbed from **9.7% to 11.9%**.

Management describes **three growth engines**: the telecom core, where exclusive device bundles are lifting revenue per user; the **home business, growing 16%**; and the **enterprise business**, growing at double digits on **AI-related IT projects and AI data centre work** — including a partnership with **GMI Cloud**, which holds NVIDIA Cloud Partner priority allocation, to package **GPU compute with dedicated network lines and carrier-grade security**. Meanwhile **momo has returned to revenue growth for two consecutive months** after a difficult stretch against Shopee and Coupang.

The cash generation is characteristic of a telecom: **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$10.74bn against NT$4.53bn of net income** — more than **2.3×**, because network depreciation is enormous. That funds a dividend of **NT$4.74** for FY2025, a **4.16% yield** at NT$114.00.

The honest qualifications: **the payout is effectively 100% of earnings** (NT$4.74 against NT$4.77), so nothing is retained; the **debt ratio of 57.77%** is meaningfully higher than FarEasTone's 45.96%, reflecting both the merger and momo's working capital; and the shares trade at **23.1× earnings and 3.79× book**. The honest read: **the best-performing of Taiwan's three carriers on returns, running an e-commerce business that distorts every margin comparison — priced for continuation, retaining nothing.**

Taiwan Mobile was founded in **1997**, when Taiwan opened mobile telecommunications to private operators. Like FarEasTone, it entered a market where the state incumbent held the best spectrum and infrastructure, and where **scale would determine profitability** — because a national mobile network costs roughly the same to build and run whether six million or ten million people use it. It **listed in 2002**.

Its distinguishing decision came later, and it was not about telecommunications. Taiwan Mobile built and retained a substantial stake in **momo**, which grew into **Taiwan's largest business-to-consumer e-commerce platform**, operating a satellite warehouse network for fast delivery. That gave the group something neither of its carrier rivals has: **a large consumer retail business alongside the network**.

The strategic logic is real — customer overlap, payment and logistics integration, bundled digital services — and the accounting consequence is severe. **E-commerce revenue is large and low-margin**; mobile subscription revenue is smaller and high-margin. Consolidating both means the group's **gross margin (21.6%) sits far below a pure carrier's (FarEasTone at 33.0%)** while its **return on equity (16.61%) sits above it**. Anyone comparing Taiwanese telecoms on gross margin without knowing this reaches the wrong conclusion.

The industry's turning point arrived with **5G**. The investment required made Taiwan's five-operator market unsustainable, and consolidation followed: **Taiwan Mobile merged with Taiwan Star on 1 December 2023**, while FarEasTone absorbed Asia Pacific Telecom. The merger gave Taiwan Mobile **100 MHz in the 5G 3.5GHz band — the widest holding of any Taiwanese carrier** — and eliminated a price-led competitor from the market. Notably, momo's presence complicated the regulatory approval, since the combination raised questions the pure-carrier merger did not.

What has followed is a company describing itself in **three parts** — telecom, home, and enterprise — with the enterprise business increasingly built around **AI infrastructure and services** rather than connectivity alone.

- **1997 (25 Feb)** — Taiwan Mobile founded as Taiwan liberalises mobile telecommunications.
- **2002 (26 Aug)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (3045)**.
- **2000s–2010s** — Establishes itself as the **second of three major carriers**; builds and retains a controlling position in **momo**, which becomes Taiwan's largest B2C e-commerce platform. Dividends held at **NT$5.6** from 2014 to 2017.
- **2020–2023** — Dividends settle at **NT$4.3** through the 5G investment cycle.
- **2023 (1 Dec)** — **Merger with Taiwan Star completes**, taking Taiwan's mobile market from five operators to three and giving Taiwan Mobile **100 MHz in the 5G 3.5GHz band** — the widest of any carrier. momo's presence within the group complicated the regulatory approval process.
- **2022** — **FY2022 EPS NT$3.91**; dividend **NT$4.3**.
- **2023** — **FY2023 EPS NT$4.33**; dividend **NT$4.3**.
- **2024** — **FY2024 EPS NT$4.57**; dividend raised to **NT$4.5**; operating margin **9.7%** in Q4.
- **2025** — **FY2025 EPS NT$4.77**; dividend **NT$4.74**; operating margin climbs to **10.6–11.1%**.
- **2026Q1** — **EPS NT$1.37 (+13%)**; operating margin **11.9%**; operating cash flow **NT$10.74bn** against **NT$4.53bn** of net profit.
- **2026 (Jan–Apr)** — Revenue **NT$65.45bn**, operating profit **+17% to NT$7.92bn**, net profit **+19% to NT$5.57bn**, **EPS NT$1.84**. Three growth engines cited: telecom ARPU, **home business +16%**, and **enterprise on AI IT and AI data centre work**; **momo returns to revenue growth for two consecutive months**. Partnership announced with **GMI Cloud** — which holds NVIDIA Cloud Partner priority allocation — packaging **GPU compute with dedicated network lines and carrier-grade security**.

Taiwan Mobile's accounts require **one structural adjustment before any comparison is valid**.

- **The margin distortion, stated first.** Gross margin is **21.6%**, against **33.0% at FarEasTone**. This is **not** evidence of a weaker telecom business — it is the arithmetic consequence of **consolidating momo's large, low-margin e-commerce revenue** into a group whose telecom revenue carries high margins. **Return on equity tells the opposite story: 16.61% against FarEasTone's 14.35%.** Any comparison of Taiwanese carriers on gross margin, without this adjustment, is wrong.
- **Steady, compounding earnings.** Annual EPS: **NT$3.91 (FY2022) → 4.33 (FY2023) → 4.57 (FY2024) → NT$4.77 (FY2025)**, with **2026Q1 at NT$1.37, up 13%**. For **January–April 2026, operating profit rose 17% to NT$7.92bn and net profit 19% to NT$5.57bn**, EPS **NT$1.84** — accelerating.
- **Margins improving with merger synergies.** Operating margin: **9.7% (2024Q4) → 10.7% → 10.9% → 11.1% → 10.6% → 11.9% (2026Q1)**. The Taiwan Star integration is showing where it should.
- **Cash generation far above accounting profit.** **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$10.74bn against NT$4.53bn of net income** — a ratio above **2.3×**, driven by depreciation on spectrum and network assets. This is the financial engine that funds both capital spending and the dividend.
- **The payout is effectively everything.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$5.6 (2014–2017) → 5.55 → 4.75 → NT$4.3 (2020–2023) → 4.5 (2024) → NT$4.74 (2025)**. Against FY2025 EPS of **NT$4.77**, that is a payout of roughly **99%**. Conventional for Taiwanese telecoms, which fund capital spending from depreciation — but **nothing is retained**, so the **4.16% yield** grows only as fast as earnings.
- **More leveraged than its rival.** **NT$236.42bn of assets** on **NT$99.85bn of equity** — a **57.77% debt ratio**, against FarEasTone's **45.96%** — reflecting both the Taiwan Star acquisition and momo's retail working capital. **NT$10.06bn of cash.**
- **Valuation.** **23.1× earnings and 3.79× book** at NT$114.00 — slightly cheaper than FarEasTone on both measures, for a higher return on equity.

The financing reality: **the better-returning of Taiwan's two private carriers, carrying more debt and a retail business that makes its margins unreadable at face value — distributing essentially all of its earnings.**

**Stance: Taiwan's second carrier, earning a higher return on equity than its listed rival at a slightly lower multiple — with an e-commerce business that distorts every margin comparison and a payout that retains nothing.**

The bull case:

1. **Consolidation delivered.** The **December 2023 Taiwan Star merger** took the market from five operators to three, removed a price-led competitor, and gave Taiwan Mobile **100 MHz in the 5G 3.5GHz band — the widest of any carrier**. Operating margin has risen **from 9.7% to 11.9%**.
2. **Accelerating results.** **January–April 2026 operating profit +17% and net profit +19%**, EPS **NT$1.84**; **2026Q1 EPS up 13%**. Annual EPS has risen every year from **NT$3.91 to NT$4.77**.
3. **Three engines, not one.** The telecom core lifting revenue per user; the **home business growing 16%**; and the **enterprise business growing at double digits on AI IT projects and AI data centre work** — including the **GMI Cloud** partnership packaging **GPU compute with dedicated lines**, a genuinely differentiated offering from a carrier.
4. **Better returns than the rival.** **16.61% ROE against FarEasTone's 14.35%**, at **23.1× earnings and 3.79× book** versus 26.9× and 3.99×.
5. **Exceptional cash generation.** **NT$10.74bn of operating cash flow against NT$4.53bn of net income**.

The counter-arguments:

- **Nothing is retained.** A payout of roughly **99%** of earnings. The dividend can only grow as fast as profit, and there is no accumulating buffer.
- **More leverage.** A **57.77% debt ratio** against FarEasTone's **45.96%**, reflecting the acquisition and momo's retail working capital.
- **momo is a mixed asset.** It has only just **returned to growth for two consecutive months** after a difficult period against Shopee and Coupang — as its own profile in this collection documents.
- **Synergies are finite.** Merger benefits are largely one-time; future growth must come from enterprise and services.
- **The margins cannot be read at face value**, which makes the company harder to analyse than a pure carrier.

A **quality-consolidation** thesis: the better operator of Taiwan's two private carriers, bought slightly cheaper — provided the analysis adjusts for momo before comparing anything.

Taiwan Mobile operates **three businesses inside one listed company**, and they have very different economics:

- **Telecom (the profit engine).** Mobile subscriptions, with **5G migration** lifting revenue per user, supported by the widest **100 MHz holding in the 5G 3.5GHz band** following the Taiwan Star merger. Network costs are largely fixed, so subscribers above break-even are highly profitable — which is why consolidation from five operators to three mattered so much.
- **Home.** Broadband, cable and household services, growing **16%** — a stable, recurring business that shares infrastructure with the mobile network.
- **Enterprise.** Corporate connectivity, IT services, cloud and increasingly **AI infrastructure**. Growing at double digits on **AICT projects and AI data centre work**, including the **GMI Cloud** partnership — which holds **NVIDIA Cloud Partner priority allocation** — packaging **GPU compute with dedicated network lines and carrier-grade security** as a single service. A carrier can offer the network and security layer that a pure cloud provider cannot.
- **momo — and why it changes the arithmetic.** As Taiwan's largest B2C e-commerce platform, momo generates **large revenue at retail margins**. Consolidating it pulls the group's **gross margin down to 21.6%** against a pure carrier's **33.0%** — not because telecom is weaker, but because **merchandise revenue simply carries less margin than subscription revenue**. It also adds retail working capital, contributing to the **57.77% debt ratio**. momo has recently **returned to revenue growth for two consecutive months** after a hard period.
- **The financial shape.** Recurring subscription receipts, enormous **depreciation on spectrum and network assets**, and therefore **operating cash flow of NT$10.74bn against NT$4.53bn of net income** — the pattern that lets a telecom distribute essentially all its accounting earnings while still investing.

The levers are **subscriber numbers and revenue per user, home and enterprise growth, momo's recovery, and network cost efficiency**. The strength is a consolidated three-player market with a genuine second and third growth engine. The vulnerability is that **the consolidated accounts do not read like a telecom's**, and every ratio must be interpreted with momo in mind.

Taiwanese telecommunications became a three-player industry in December 2023, and the three players are no longer competing only in telecommunications.

- **The consolidation.** For years Taiwan supported five mobile operators for 23 million people. **5G investment requirements ended that**: **Taiwan Mobile absorbed Taiwan Star** and **FarEasTone absorbed Asia Pacific Telecom**, both completing in **December 2023**. Market shares settled at roughly **Chunghwa Telecom 37.6%, Taiwan Mobile 32%, FarEasTone 30.4%**.
- **Why three is much better than five.** Network businesses have enormous fixed costs, so sub-scale operators compete on price and destroy industry returns. Removing two of them stabilised pricing — visible in **Taiwan Mobile's operating margin rising from 9.7% to 11.9%** and in FarEasTone's parallel improvement.
- **Where growth actually is.** Not subscribers — Taiwan's population is flat and penetration complete. Growth comes from **5G migration to higher-value plans**, **home services**, and above all **enterprise ICT, cloud and AI**. All three carriers are pursuing the same expansion, which is where they now genuinely compete — and where they face systems integrators and global cloud providers rather than each other.
- **The AI infrastructure angle.** Carriers own something cloud providers do not: **the network, and the security and reliability guarantees that come with it**. Taiwan Mobile's **GMI Cloud** partnership — combining **GPU compute with dedicated lines and carrier-grade security** — is an attempt to convert that into a differentiated AI offering, alongside data centre projects.
- **What makes Taiwan Mobile structurally different.** It is the only carrier that also owns a major e-commerce platform. That gives it consumer reach, payment and logistics assets — and **an accounting profile no other carrier shares**, which is why direct margin comparisons across the three fail.
- **Regulation.** Spectrum, pricing and competition are all regulated, and merger approval took extensive review — with momo's presence in the group adding complexity that the pure-carrier merger did not face.

Taiwan Mobile's position is **strong and structurally second**, with the highest return on equity of the two listed private carriers. The industry truth is that **Taiwanese telecoms have stopped competing on connectivity price and started competing on enterprise services** — a contest of capability rather than scale.

**Strengths**
- **Taiwan Star merger (Dec 2023)** delivered synergies: operating margin **9.7% → 11.9%**; **100 MHz in 5G 3.5GHz** — the widest holding.
- **Accelerating results**: Jan–Apr 2026 operating profit **+17%**, net profit **+19%**, **EPS NT$1.84**; **ROE 16.61%**, above FarEasTone's 14.35%.
- **Three growth engines**: telecom ARPU, **home +16%**, and enterprise on **AI IT and AI data centre** work, including the **GMI Cloud** GPU-plus-network offering.
- **Exceptional cash generation**: operating cash flow **NT$10.74bn** against **NT$4.53bn** of net income; **4.16% yield**.

**Weaknesses**
- **Payout of roughly 99%** of earnings — nothing retained.
- **57.77% debt ratio** against FarEasTone's **45.96%**.
- **Gross margin of 21.6% is not comparable** to a pure carrier's — momo's consolidation makes every margin ratio require adjustment.
- **momo has only just returned to growth** after a difficult stretch against Shopee and Coupang.

**Opportunities**
- **Enterprise AI infrastructure** — GPU compute with dedicated lines and carrier-grade security.
- **5G migration** and home services lifting revenue per user.
- momo's recovery adding a second growth vector.

**Threats**
- **Synergies are finite** — one-time merger benefits largely captured.
- **E-commerce competition** from Shopee and Coupang pressing momo.
- Direct competition with FarEasTone and Chunghwa in enterprise services; regulatory intervention on pricing or spectrum.

- **The accounts cannot be compared at face value (the analytical risk).** Taiwan Mobile's **21.6% gross margin** against **FarEasTone's 33.0%** does not mean its telecom business is worse — it means **momo's low-margin e-commerce revenue is consolidated**. Its **return on equity of 16.61% exceeds FarEasTone's 14.35%**. Any screen or comparison using gross margin across Taiwanese carriers will rank this company incorrectly.
- **Nothing is retained.** The payout is roughly **99% of earnings** (**NT$4.74 against NT$4.77**). Conventional for a Taiwanese telecom funding capital spending from depreciation — but it means the dividend grows only with earnings, no buffer accumulates, and any earnings setback flows straight to the payout.
- **Higher leverage than the rival.** A **57.77% debt ratio** against FarEasTone's **45.96%**, on **NT$236.42bn of assets**. This reflects the Taiwan Star acquisition and momo's retail working capital — manageable given the cash generation, but a real difference.
- **Merger synergies are finite.** The improvement from **9.7% to 11.9%** operating margin came largely from eliminating duplicated network and overhead costs. Those gains happen once; from here growth must come from enterprise services and home.
- **momo's competitive position.** Taiwan's e-commerce market is contested by **Shopee and Coupang**, and momo has only just **returned to growth for two consecutive months**. Its own profile in this collection records a difficult multi-year stretch.
- **Enterprise AI is a contested market.** The **GMI Cloud** partnership is differentiated, but carriers competing in AI infrastructure face global cloud providers and systems integrators with far deeper capabilities.

Taiwan Mobile's outlook depends on **whether the enterprise and home engines can take over as merger synergies are exhausted — and whether momo's recovery holds.** The axes to watch:

- **Operating margin.** Up from **9.7% to 11.9%** since the merger, and the clearest measure of synergy realisation. Continued expansion means integration benefits are still flowing; a plateau means the story now rests entirely on services growth.
- **Enterprise revenue and the AI offering.** Growing at double digits on **AICT and AI data centre work**, with the **GMI Cloud** partnership packaging **GPU compute with dedicated lines and carrier-grade security**. This is the only growth avenue not constrained by Taiwan's saturated consumer market, and the one that would justify the multiple.
- **momo's trajectory.** **Two consecutive months of revenue growth** after a hard period. Sustained recovery adds a genuine second engine; renewed weakness drags the consolidated result and further muddies the margins.
- **Home business growth.** Running at **+16%** — stable, recurring, and sharing infrastructure with the mobile network.
- **The dividend.** **NT$4.74 for FY2025** at roughly a **99% payout**. It can only rise with earnings, so it is a direct readout of profit progress — and **January–April operating profit up 17%** is a promising start.

Bottom line: Taiwan Mobile solved its scale problem by **merging with Taiwan Star in December 2023**, emerging with **the widest 5G 3.5GHz holding in Taiwan**, an operating margin up **from 9.7% to 11.9%**, **January–April 2026 operating profit up 17% and net profit up 19%**, and the **highest return on equity (16.61%) of Taiwan's two listed private carriers** — at **23.1× earnings and 3.79× book**, slightly cheaper than its rival. It also **retains none of its earnings**, carries **more debt (57.77%)**, and owns an **e-commerce business that makes its 21.6% gross margin look far worse than it is**. Judge it on **operating margin, enterprise growth and return on equity** — and never on gross margin without adjusting for momo first.
